We've seen numerous examples showing that granting Meta's Muse app full disk access on Mac is a terrible idea, and now another major privacy issue has come to light. The latest discovery reveals that Muse analyses your communications with every person in your life on an hourly basis.

Apple has expressed grave concern about this development, stating in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "Full Disk Access" feature to prevent such issues from occurring……

Meta's Muse app forces authorities to act swiftly

Meta recently launched its Muse personal AI agent app for iPhone and Mac. Despite it being clearly unwise to allow a Meta app unrestricted access to all the data on your Apple device, the app quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, the good times didn't last, and problems soon began to escalate significantly. Things have not improved since. Wired magazine reports that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered Meta has instructed Muse to extract all the data needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be enabling it to "create a dedicated page for every person" in the user's life. The instruction states that this hourly process collects data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "partners," and people you "follow." [……] The instructions read: "Where they live, what they do for work, recurring topics (moving, shared savings goals)." The instructions further note that the model can record "important dates" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history log may contain context such as "trips in March, resolved arguments, milestones from last week."

Apple tightens controls over Full Disk Access permissions

You might assume that the prompt for granting an app Full Disk Access on Mac explains everything, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users have granted this all-access pass without realising just how dangerous this step is.

Apple says the feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers have since applied it to many more uses, including AI agents. The company has stated it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

Here's what Apple must do—and must never do

Apple says taking this step is "crucial," and I completely agree. When existing permission requests fail to adequately convey the gravity of what you're authorising, Apple must make sure users truly understand what they're allowing. This is essential.

What I'd like to see is clearer text advising users not to do this unless they're certain they understand the consequences. Something along the lines of:

Basically, the stronger the wording, the better. I'd also be fine with a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Popular comment by Rayz2023

Do you really think the kind of people who would grant disk-level access to a Meta app are the type who would sit down and read more than two lines of text?

That said, Apple absolutely must not repeat past mistakes, like the one it made with screen recording permissions in macOS Sequoia. Of course, that's also extremely dangerous, and strong warnings are appropriate—but what Apple did at the time was force us to confirm these permissions every week, and again every time the system restarted.

This move was widely criticised for turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, Apple already overreaches when it occasionally asks for repeated permission confirmations on iPhone. For example, I've granted Citymapper access to my location so it can continue providing navigation in the background—and Apple, I really don't need you to confirm whether I still want to do that.

Yes, issue the strongest possible warning when granting Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect that decision. Thanks, and no more weekly or other mandatory confirmations.
